title: Google Opens SynthID Detector to Everyone, With Partner Watermark Checks
excerpt: Previously limited to journalists and researchers, Google's watermark checker at synthid.com now scans images, video and audio for Google, OpenAI, NVIDIA and Kakao watermarks — but it is not a universal AI detector.
body:
• Google opened the SynthID Detector to everyone worldwide on October 7-8, 2026, at synthid.com, after limiting it to journalists, media professionals and researchers since its May 2025 preview at I/O.
  • The portal checks images, video and audio for invisible SynthID watermarks, and now also detects partner watermarks from OpenAI, NVIDIA and Kakao, with Apple support coming soon.
  • Google says more than 180 billion images and videos have been watermarked, along with 240,000 years of audio, and built-in checks in Search, Gemini and Chrome handle about 1 million verification requests a day.
  • Reader check: you can upload a JPG, PNG, WEBP, MP4, MP3 or WAV file at synthid.com for a free check, but a "not detected" result does not prove content is human-made — the tool only finds SynthID-carrying media.

Google has made its SynthID Detector publicly available worldwide, allowing anyone to upload an image, video or audio clip and check whether it carries an invisible watermark associated with generative AI. The tool was previously limited to selected journalists, media professionals and researchers, according to PetaPixel. Google opened it globally in English on October 7, 2026, Unite.AI reported, in an announcement written by Pushmeet Kohli, vice president of science and strategic initiatives at Google DeepMind.

What the Detector Actually Checks

SynthID, introduced in 2023, embeds imperceptible watermarks directly into AI-generated media at the moment of creation — in the pixels of images and video and in the frequency components of audio, rather than in metadata that can be stripped away. Google uses it across products including Nano Banana, Veo, Lyria and Gemini, as well as Flow, ProducerAI and Vids. The public portal supports common formats including JPG, PNG, WEBP and GIF for images, MP4 and MOV for video, and MP3, WAV and FLAC for audio.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=fBnrZaM6Ohw

The expansion beyond Google is the substantive change. The detector now also recognises watermarks from partners OpenAI, NVIDIA and Kakao, and some reports also list ElevenLabs among partners extending SynthID watermarking. Apple has announced plans to adopt SynthID, although Google has not given a date for when Apple-made content will be detectable. For images the portal reports whether a watermark is present; for video and audio it can identify which segments are watermarked.

Scale, and Why Watermarks Survive Editing

Google says it has watermarked more than 180 billion images and videos since 2023, along with 240,000 years of audio content. Detection is already built into Search, the Gemini app and Chrome, which together handle roughly 1 million verification requests a day. The watermarks are designed to remain detectable after cropping, added filters, frame-rate changes and lossy compression for images and video, and after added noise, MP3 compression and changes in playback speed for audio.

Testing cited by PetaPixel illustrates both the reach and the nuance. CNET found that an iPhone photo adjusted using Apple's Reframe tool was flagged as containing a SynthID watermark, while an unedited iPhone photograph was not. In other words, the system can pick up AI-assisted edits, not only fully generated media.

"This is not a general AI detector."

— SynthID Detector FAQ, via Unite.AI

The Limit: A Clue, Not a Verdict

Google is explicit about the boundary. The detector can identify only media from companies that have adopted SynthID. Content made with a non-participating model, or content with no watermark, will return a negative result even if it was generated by AI, and heavy modification can degrade the signal. The site also notes rare false triggers and recommends uploading the highest-quality file available and gathering multiple points of evidence before reaching a conclusion.

That makes the tool most useful as a first check in a wider provenance workflow, alongside reverse image search, source verification and, where available, content credentials. Uploaded files, Google says, are processed in real time and deleted after results are displayed, while a digital signature linked to the user is kept for 24 hours to enforce daily quotas; some users have reported a limit of about 10 checks a day on the free portal.

What This Means for Readers

For diaspora readers who routinely receive forwarded images, election material and family-media claims on messaging apps, the practical step is simple: save the original file, not a screenshot, and run it through synthid.com before forwarding it as fact. A positive result is strong evidence the file was made or edited with a participating AI tool. A negative result settles nothing on its own. TIME has named SynthID one of its Best Inventions of 2026, but its value will depend on how many rival labs adopt the same watermark — which is why the partner expansion, more than the public launch itself, is the development to watch.
